title: Read File (Deprecated)
description: Read the complete contents of a file as text. DEPRECATED: Use read_text_file instead.

path.description: The file to read as text. Absolute, or relative to an allowed directory; it must resolve inside the allowed directories.

tail.description: If provided, returns only the last N lines of the file

head.description: If provided, returns only the first N lines of the file

title: Read Text File
description: Read the complete contents of a file from the file system as text. Handles various text encodings and provides detailed error messages if the file cannot be read. Use this tool when you need to examine the contents of a single file. Use the 'head' parameter to read only the first N lines of a file, or the 'tail' parameter to read only the last N lines of a file. Operates on the file as text regardless of extension. Only works within allowed directories.

path.description: The file to read as text. Absolute, or relative to an allowed directory; it must resolve inside the allowed directories.

tail.description: If provided, returns only the last N lines of the file

head.description: If provided, returns only the first N lines of the file

title: Read Media File
description: Read a file and return it as a base64-encoded content block with its MIME type. Image and audio files are returned as image/audio content; any other file type is returned as an embedded resource. Only works within allowed directories.

path.description: The image, audio or other file to read as base64. Absolute, or relative to an allowed directory; it must resolve inside the allowed directories.

title: Read Multiple Files
description: Read the contents of multiple files simultaneously. This is more efficient than reading files one by one when you need to analyze or compare multiple files. Each file's content is returned with its path as a reference. Failed reads for individual files won't stop the entire operation. Only works within allowed directories.

paths.description: Array of file paths to read. Each path must be a string pointing to a valid file within allowed directories.

title: Write File
description: Create a new file or completely overwrite an existing file with new content. Use with caution as it will overwrite existing files without warning. Handles text content with proper encoding. Only works within allowed directories.

path.description: The file to create, or to overwrite if it exists; its parent directory must exist. Absolute, or relative to an allowed directory; it must resolve inside the allowed directories.

content.description: The complete text the file will contain, replacing any it had

title: Append File
description: Append text to the end of a file, creating the file if it does not exist. The existing content is never changed or replaced. The text is appended exactly as given, with no newline added before or after it, so end it with a newline if the next append should start on a new line. Only works within allowed directories.

path.description: The file to append to; it is created if it does not exist. Absolute, or relative to an allowed directory; it must resolve inside the allowed directories.

content.description: Text to append, exactly as given. No newline is added: end it with \n if the next append should start on a new line.

title: Edit File
description: Make line-based edits to a text file. Edits apply in order, each to the result of the ones before it, and each replaces the first match of its oldText with newText. oldText must match the file's text exactly, except that line endings (LF or CRLF) never matter and, when there is no exact match, a run of whole lines matches if each line is equal once leading and trailing whitespace is ignored (newText then takes the file's indentation). Whitespace inside a line must match. If any edit has no match, nothing is written and the error shows the closest lines of the file, numbered, to copy oldText from. Returns a git-style diff showing the changes made. Only works within allowed directories.

path.description: The text file to edit. Absolute, or relative to an allowed directory; it must resolve inside the allowed directories.

oldText.description: Text to search for - must match exactly

edits.description: The replacements to make, applied in order, each to the result of the ones before it. If any one has no match, none is written.

dryRun.description: Preview changes using git-style diff format

title: Create Directory
description: Create a new directory or ensure a directory exists. Can create multiple nested directories in one operation. If the directory already exists, this operation will succeed silently. Perfect for setting up directory structures for projects or ensuring required paths exist. Only works within allowed directories.

path.description: The directory to create, with any missing parents; an existing directory is left as is. Absolute, or relative to an allowed directory; it must resolve inside the allowed directories.

title: List Directory
description: List the files and directories directly inside a path, each marked [FILE] or [DIR]. Use it to see what a directory contains; when you also need each entry's size or want entries sorted by size, use list_directory_with_sizes instead, and for a recursive view use directory_tree. Returns one line per entry. Only works within allowed directories.

path.description: The directory to list. Absolute, or relative to an allowed directory; it must resolve inside the allowed directories.

title: List Directory with Sizes
description: List the files and directories directly inside a path with each file's size, marked [FILE] or [DIR], sorted by name or by size, largest first (sortBy). Use it when sizes matter, such as finding the largest files; for names only, use list_directory, which returns less text. Returns one line per entry, followed by the totals. Only works within allowed directories.

path.description: The directory to list. Absolute, or relative to an allowed directory; it must resolve inside the allowed directories.

sortBy.description: Sort entries by name or size

title: Directory Tree
description: Get a recursive tree view of files and directories as a JSON structure. Each entry includes 'name', 'type' (file/directory), and 'children' for directories. Files have no children array, while directories always have a children array (which may be empty), except at the last level when 'depth' limits the tree: those directories are not read and have no children array. The output is formatted with 2-space indentation for readability. Only works within allowed directories.

path.description: The directory at the root of the tree. Absolute, or relative to an allowed directory; it must resolve inside the allowed directories.

excludePatterns.description: Patterns for entries to leave out, with their contents, matched against each entry's path relative to path. A pattern with no '*' matches that name at any depth ('node_modules' leaves out every node_modules directory); a pattern with '*' is a glob matched as written, and one ending in '/**' also leaves out the directory it names.

depth.description: How many levels to descend: 1 lists only the entries directly in path. Directories at the last level have no children array. Omit for the whole tree.

title: Move File
description: Move or rename files and directories. Can move files between directories and rename them in a single operation. If the destination exists, the operation will fail. Works across different directories and can be used for simple renaming within the same directory. Both source and destination must be within allowed directories.

source.description: The file or directory to move or rename. Absolute, or relative to an allowed directory; it must resolve inside the allowed directories.

destination.description: Its new path, including the name; nothing may exist there yet. Absolute, or relative to an allowed directory; it must resolve inside the allowed directories.

title: Copy File
description: Copy a file to a new location, without reading its content into the conversation. Copies one regular file, keeping its permissions and modification time; directories are not copied. If the destination exists, the operation will fail: it never overwrites. Both source and destination must be within allowed directories.

destination.description: Where to create the copy; nothing may exist there yet

title: Search Files
description: Find files and directories by NAME, not by content: this tool never reads or searches inside files. It walks the tree under 'path' and matches a glob pattern against each entry's path relative to 'path' (case-sensitive). Use '*.ext' to match entries directly under 'path', and '**/*.ext' or '**/name' to match at any depth. Returns full paths to all matching items. Great for finding files when you don't know their exact location. Only searches within allowed directories.

path.description: The directory to search under. Absolute, or relative to an allowed directory; it must resolve inside the allowed directories.

pattern.description: Glob matched against each entry's path relative to path, never its content: '*.ts' matches directly under path, '**/*.ts' at any depth.

excludePatterns.description: Patterns for entries to leave out, with their contents, matched against each entry's path relative to path. A pattern with no '*' matches that name at any depth ('node_modules' leaves out every node_modules directory); a pattern with '*' is a glob matched as written, and one ending in '/**' also leaves out the directory it names.

title: Get File Info
description: Retrieve detailed metadata about a file or directory. Returns comprehensive information including size, creation time, last modified time, permissions, type and hard-link count. This tool is perfect for understanding file characteristics without reading the actual content. Only works within allowed directories.

path.description: The file or directory to describe. Absolute, or relative to an allowed directory; it must resolve inside the allowed directories.

title: List Allowed Directories
description: Returns the list of directories that this server is allowed to access. Subdirectories within these allowed directories are also accessible. Use this to understand which directories and their nested paths are available before trying to access files.

title: Create Files
description: Write whole text files (new, overwrite, or append) and create empty directories, with missing parents. Use when you have full content or need folders. Do not use it for partial edits; use `edit`, `replace_text`, or `patch` instead, and `move` to copy or rename. Whole-file writes are atomic (temp file, then rename); appends are not. An existing file is replaced only with overwrite: true or after one user confirmation for the batch; nothing is written before the answer. Declined entries fail with CANCELLED; skipped ones land in skipped. Entries fail alone; the call errors only when all fail. Returns files (path, size, lineCount, mimeType, kind, resourceUri, created, modified), directories, failures, skipped, and an undo id for `undo` (30 min), or undoUnavailable.

files.description: Files to write. Give files, directories, or both. Combined content per call is at most FS_MAX_FILE_SIZE (default 10 MiB).

path.description: Absolute file path inside a writable root; one entry per file.

content.description: Full text to write, verbatim, as UTF-8.

append.description: Add content to the end, adding no newline; creates a missing file. Never asks; wins over overwrite. lineCount is 0 past FS_MAX_FILE_SIZE.

overwrite.description: Replace an existing file without asking. Without it, a client that cannot show the prompt fails the whole call with INVALID_INPUT.

directories.description: Empty directories, created recursively; an existing directory succeeds; a path also listed in files is rejected.

items.description: File or directory path inside an allowed workspace root.

title: Delete Paths
description: Delete files, directories, and symlinks. Use when a path should no longer exist. Do not use it to rename or relocate; use `move` instead, and `undo` to restore. A symlink is removed, never its target. A non-empty directory needs `recursive: true`, else that path fails INVALID_INPUT, and user confirmation; nothing is deleted until all are answered, and a client that cannot prompt fails the whole call INVALID_INPUT. Deleting a folder that holds protected files cannot be undone. Otherwise each path fails alone (ACCESS_DENIED: root, read-only, outside; CANCELLED: refused or changed; INVALID_INPUT: nested pair). Returns per-path { deleted } or { error } (a skipped prompt gives deleted: false), a summary, and an undo id valid 30 minutes, or undoUnavailable with the reason.

items.description: File or directory path inside an allowed workspace root.

paths.description: Exact paths (no globs): files, directories, or symlinks. Duplicates collapse

recursive.description: Required for a non-empty directory, else INVALID_INPUT.

ignoreIfNotExists.description: True: a missing path returns deleted: true instead of failing NOT_FOUND

title: Diff
description: Compare two text files and return a unified diff from a to b. Use when you need line differences between two files on disk. Do not use it to find text across files; use `search_text` instead. To preview your own pending change, use the dryRun option of the write tools. Neither file is changed. Binary and non-UTF-8 files fail. A file over the size limit fails with TOO_LARGE. So does a diff not done within 1 s, or a full diff queue; retry once, then `read` matching line ranges. a is the - side and b the + side; swap them to reverse the diff. context only sets how many unchanged lines surround each hunk, not what counts as a change. Returns ---/+++ headers (basenames) and @@ hunks; identical files give headers only.

a.description: Original file; its lines are the - side

b.description: Changed file; its lines are the + side

context.description: Unchanged lines shown around each hunk; output size only

title: Edit Files
description: Replace exact, unique text snippets in up to 5 existing text files. Use when you know the exact text to change. Do not use it for every match of a pattern; use `replace_text` instead. To apply a unified diff, use `patch`; for a new file or a whole rewrite, use `create`. Each file is all or nothing: an unmatched or ambiguous oldText writes nothing to that file, and other files still run; dryRun reports unmatched text instead of failing. Missing, binary, non-UTF-8, and over-size-cap (default 10 MiB) files fail. Returns one summary line per file (+added -removed, NO MATCH, or FAILED); a dry run appends unified diffs. With undo enabled, live runs add an undo id for `undo`, valid 30 minutes.

path.description: One file to edit; give edits with it. Not allowed with files

edits.description: Replacements for path, applied in order; each oldText is matched against the text the earlier edits left. Required with path

oldText.description: Exact text to find. It must match exactly once, so include 3-5 lines of context. Several matches fail and list up to 5 line numbers.

newText.description: Replacement text. Use an empty string to delete the matched oldText.

files.description: Batch mode: one entry per file, each with its own edits

path.description: File to edit; each file appears once

oldText.description: Exact text to find. It must match exactly once, so include 3-5 lines of context. Several matches fail and list up to 5 line numbers.

newText.description: Replacement text. Use an empty string to delete the matched oldText.

edits.description: Replacements for this file, applied in order; each oldText is matched against the text the earlier edits left

dryRun.description: Write nothing; return a unified diff per file. An unmatched oldText is reported instead of failing; an ambiguous one still fails

ignoreWhitespace.description: Match oldText ignoring indentation and spacing, never across line breaks; newText is re-indented to the match

title: List
description: List a directory inside the roots as a name tree, walking up to maxDepth levels. Use when you need to see what a folder holds. Do not use it to find files by name or glob; use `find_files` instead, `read` or `search_text` for contents, `stat` for one path. Skips hidden entries, .gitignore matches, and build and tool folders unless includeHidden or includeIgnored is set, naming the ignore-rule folders it hid. Folders at maxDepth are shown, but their contents are not listed or counted. At most 20,000 entries are kept. A timeout returns a partial result with stoppedReason. Errors: NOT_DIRECTORY for a file, ACCESS_DENIED outside the roots. Returns tree text, entries[{name, relativePath, type, size?}], totalEntries/Files/Directories, unexpandedDirectories, skippedInaccessible, and when cut nextCursor and resourceUri (about 60 s).

path.description: Directory to list (default: the only root; required with several roots)

maxDepth.description: Levels to walk; 1 = direct children. Directories at the limit are shown, not expanded.

maxEntries.description: Entries per page; changing it keeps a cursor valid

includeIgnored.description: Include .gitignore matches and build and tool folders (node_modules, .git, dist, build, out, tmp, coverage)

includeSizes.description: Show file sizes and a totals line in the tree (stats every file, slower on big trees)

sortBy.description: Order within each directory, after directories (size: largest file first; sizes appear only with includeSizes)

cursor.description: Opaque pagination cursor. Pass it unchanged for the next page. Pages come from one snapshot taken on the first call. It expires after ~60s; if rejected, retry without a cursor.

title: Move or Copy Files
description: Move, rename, or copy files and directories inside the roots. Use when you need to rename, relocate, or duplicate (copy: true). Do not use to change contents (`edit`, `patch`) or remove paths (`delete`). Missing parents are created. An existing destination asks to confirm; declining cancels the call, skipping drops that pair. Only copies can bypass the prompt (overwrite: true). A directory move never merges into a non-empty directory; a copy merges. Pairs that share a destination or overlap another pair fail; run dependent moves separately. Returns summary lines naming each pair and failure, and { moves: [{ from, to }], failures?, skipped?, undo id for `undo` (30 minutes) or undoUnavailable }; an error only if every pair failed.

destination.description: Full target path including the new name, not a parent folder

moves.description: Pairs run independently, with no rollback; a declined overwrite still cancels them all

copy.description: Copy and leave sources in place instead of moving

overwrite.description: Copy only: replace existing destinations without confirmation

title: Patch
description: Apply a single-file unified diff to one existing UTF-8 text file. Use when you hold a unified diff. Do not use it for one exact snippet; use `edit` instead. For pattern matches use `replace_text`; for new files, `create`. All or nothing: if any hunk mismatches its context, nothing is written; INVALID_INPUT usually names it. Header line numbers may be off. A diff of context lines only writes nothing and records no undo. File lines x diff lines over 10,000,000 fails with TOO_LARGE. Returns path, linesAdded, linesRemoved, size, lineCount, mimeType, kind, modified, resourceUri when linkable, and an undo id for `undo` (30 minutes) or undoUnavailable; dryRun adds the resulting diff.

path.description: Existing text file to patch. Overrides the ---/+++ names in diff.

diff.description: Single-file unified diff, at least one @@ hunk, hunks in file order. Multi-file diffs are rejected; a leading BOM is ignored.

dryRun.description: Check every hunk and return the resulting diff; write nothing. Counts come from the recomputed diff unless it times out.

title: Read File
description: Read one file or up to 1000, whole or as a line slice. Use when you know the path. Do not use it to check size or existence; use `stat` instead. To locate content, use `search_text`, `find_files`, or `list`. Only whole reads return images and audio as media; other binary files fail with BINARY_FILE unless binary: true. Past the size limit, a whole read fails with TOO_LARGE; a single-path head or range is truncated. A batch shares a 512 KiB budget: an overflowing file is skipped and later files still read. isError means every path failed. Pick one slice (head, tail, or startLine/endLine); it applies to every batch file. Returns text plus per-path results[]: an error, or linesRead, hasMoreLines, continuation args, modified, optional contentHash. Full reads add totalLines; a tail gets no continuation.

includeHash.description: Include SHA-256 of the returned content (the slice for a partial read).

binary.description: Return a non-image, non-audio binary file as a base64 resource. Whole reads only. Without it, such a file fails with BINARY_FILE.

lineNumbers.description: Prefix each line with its number and a tab. Not with tail. Leave the prefix out of edit text.

head.description: First N lines. Not with tail or startLine/endLine.

tail.description: Last N lines. Not with head, startLine/endLine, or lineNumbers.

startLine.description: First line, 1-based. Without endLine, reads to the end.

path.description: Single file path; mutually exclusive with paths

paths.description: Array of file paths for batch mode (max 1000); mutually exclusive with path

items.description: File or directory path inside an allowed workspace root.

title: Search and Replace
description: Replace every match of literal text or an RE2 regex in one file or across a directory tree. Use when the same change must land at every occurrence. Do not use it for one unique snippet; use `edit` instead, `patch` for a unified diff, or `search_text` to only find matches. A live run rewrites each file as the scan reaches it; one failed file does not stop the others. Reaching maxMatches (default 100), maxFiles, or the deadline stops the run; files already rewritten stay changed. Returns changed paths, failures, skip counts, stoppedReason, and an undo id (live runs, when undo is enabled) for `undo`, valid 30 minutes. isError is set when every file failed or the request is invalid (bad regex, path outside roots).

path.description: File or directory to rewrite. A named file ignores pattern, hidden, and gitignore filters, and fails if binary or too large. Omitted, it targets the ENTIRE single root (required with several roots); try a wide scope with dryRun=true first

pattern.description: Glob limiting which files under a directory path are rewritten (e.g. **/*.ts). Without /, it matches file names at any depth. Ignored when path names a file

searchPattern.description: Literal text or RE2 regex to find; can span lines. With isRegex=true, ^ and $ match per line (\A and \z for the whole file); no lookaround or backreferences. All-CRLF files match as LF: write \n.

replacement.description: Replacement text. An empty string deletes matches.

isRegex.description: Treat searchPattern as an RE2 regex and expand $1, $<name>, and $& in replacement (default: literal text match)

caseSensitive.description: Match case exactly. Unlike search_text, defaults to true.

dryRun.description: Preview without writing. Always returns the diff, never an undo id.

returnDiff.description: Include the unified diff in a live run. Cut at 20 KB.

maxMatches.description: Maximum matches replaced across all files (default: 100). Setting it makes the scan sequential and exact.

maxFiles.description: Stops after this many files scanned, counting files with no match; reports stoppedReason=maxFiles (default: no limit)

maxDepth.description: Max directory depth. 0 scans only the base directory. Omit for no limit.

title: Workspace Roots
description: List roots this server can access and its read-only directories. Use for allowed paths or after ACCESS_DENIED. Do not use it to browse; use `list`, `find_files`, or `stat` instead. Accepted grants add roots; call again after one. Outside paths prompt a grant only on elicitation clients, never for home, system paths, or anything outside FS_ROOT_BOUNDARY. Returns absolute { roots, readOnlyDirs (writes, moves, deletes refused), hint? when roots is empty }.

title: Search Content
description: Search file contents under the roots for literal text or an RE2 regex. Use when you need the files and lines that contain some text. Do not use it to find files by name; use `find_files` instead. A regex may span lines; the hit is on its first line. Skips hidden entries, .gitignore matches, and build folders unless includeHidden or includeIgnored. Lines over 1000 chars are clipped around the match. Stops early at 10000 matching lines or the timeout, setting stoppedReason. Returns root, `file:line: text` rows (a named file prints its path once), matches with column and context, totals, skip counts, nextCursor (expires after about 60 s), and resourceUri for a multi-page or stopped first page.

path.description: File or directory to search (default: the only root). A named file is searched alone: pattern, maxDepth, and hidden/ignored filtering do not apply. Result paths are relative to the root, not to path.

pattern.description: Glob limiting which files are searched: *.ts matches names at any depth, src/**/*.ts matches paths relative to path. Default: all files.

searchPattern.description: Text to find, literal unless isRegex is true. RE2 has no lookahead, lookbehind, or backreferences.

isRegex.description: Treat searchPattern as an RE2 regex

caseSensitive.description: Match case exactly. replace_text matches case by default, so pass true to preview what it will replace.

maxResults.description: Matching lines per page; context lines do not count. Later pages come via cursor.

context.description: Lines shown before and after each match, like grep -C.

maxDepth.description: Max directory depth. 0 scans only the base directory. Omit for no limit.

cursor.description: Opaque pagination cursor. Pass it unchanged for the next page. Pages come from one snapshot taken on the first call. It expires after ~60s; if rejected, retry without a cursor.

title: Find Files
description: Find files whose name or path matches a glob under a directory. Use when you know a name or path pattern but not the location. Do not use it for file contents; use `search_text` instead. To browse a folder, use `list`. Matches files, never directories. Skips hidden entries, .gitignore matches, and build folders unless includeHidden or includeIgnored. Scanning stops at 10,000 matches (stoppedReason maxResults) or the time limit (FS_TOOL_TIMEOUT_MS, default 5 s; stoppedReason timeout) and still returns what it found. path must be an existing directory; a file path is rejected. maxResults sizes a page, not the scan; page on with nextCursor (expires after about 60 s, then search again without it). Returns root, results[{ path }], totalMatches, filesScanned, and when set nextCursor, stoppedReason, skippedInaccessible (entries it could not read), excludedDirs (skipped folders: total and first 5), resourceUri (all kept matches). Paths are relative to root when unambiguous, otherwise absolute.

path.description: Existing directory to search under. Required with several roots. Patterns with / match from here.

pattern.description: Glob. Without / it matches file names at any depth (*.ts). With / it matches paths relative to path (src/**/*.ts).

maxResults.description: Files per page; totalMatches counts all kept matches.

sortBy.description: name: by file name across folders, ties by path. Sorts the first 10,000 kept matches before paging.

maxDepth.description: Max directory depth. 0 scans only the base directory. Omit for no limit.

cursor.description: Opaque pagination cursor. Pass it unchanged for the next page. Pages come from one snapshot taken on the first call. It expires after ~60s; if rejected, retry without a cursor.

title: Get File Info
description: Get metadata for files or directories. Use when you need to check existence, size, or read cost. Do not use for contents; use `read` instead, `list` for directory entries, or `find_files` to find by name. Pass `path` or `paths` (up to 1000), never both. Paths settle independently (missing gives NOT_FOUND); the call errors only if all fail. Symlinks report their own metadata, not the target's. `path` gives one result; `paths` gives one per path, in input order. Returns per-path values or errors ({ code, message }), plus summary { total, succeeded, failed }. Values hold name, path, type, size or entryCount (directories), tokenEstimate (files, bytes/4), timestamps, permissions (POSIX) or readOnly (Windows), isHidden (dot prefix), mimeType, symlinkTarget.

path.description: Single file path; mutually exclusive with paths

paths.description: Array of file paths for batch mode (max 1000); mutually exclusive with path

items.description: File or directory path inside an allowed workspace root.

title: Undo
description: Revert create, edit, replace_text, patch, move, or delete calls by undo id or the newest N calls. Use when a change made by this server must be reverted. Do not use for outside changes or expired ids; rewrite those with `edit` or `create`. Preview with dryRun, which lists ids. A path changed since that call is skipped while the rest revert; it stays under its id for a retry. The in-memory journal keeps up to 64 calls for 30 minutes, fewer when FS_MAX_UNDO_BYTES fills. No redo. Unknown ids fail NOT_FOUND. Returns steps[] of {id, tool, results[]}, each path restored or with an error code. A long list is cut (failures kept), marked truncated with totalResults. Errors only if every path fails.

id.description: Undo id from a mutating tool result. Required over HTTP, where all clients share the journal.

steps.description: Revert the newest N calls, newest first. Not with id; rejected over HTTP. Omit both to revert the newest call.

dryRun.description: Preview without changing anything. With no id or steps, previews every journaled call and lists their ids.

description: Shows the working tree status
Shows changes in the working directory that are not yet staged
Shows changes that are staged for commit
Shows differences between branches or commits, or across a revision range (main..feature, main...feature)
Records changes to the repository
Adds file contents to the staging area
Unstages all staged changes
Shows the commit logs

max_count.title: Max Count

start_timestamp.description: Start timestamp for filtering commits. Accepts: ISO 8601 format (e.g., '2024-01-15T14:30:25'), relative dates (e.g., '2 weeks ago', 'yesterday'), or absolute dates (e.g., '2024-01-15', 'Jan 15 2024')
start_timestamp.title: Start Timestamp

end_timestamp.description: End timestamp for filtering commits. Accepts: ISO 8601 format (e.g., '2024-01-15T14:30:25'), relative dates (e.g., '2 weeks ago', 'yesterday'), or absolute dates (e.g., '2024-01-15', 'Jan 15 2024')
end_timestamp.title: End Timestamp

base_branch.description: Branch, tag or commit SHA to create the branch from. Defaults to the current branch, or to the current commit when HEAD is detached
base_branch.title: Base Branch

source_branch.title: Source Branch

fast_forward_only.description: Only fast-forward, failing if the branches have diverged. False allows a merge commit
fast_forward_only.title: Fast Forward Only

List Git branches

repo_path.description: The path to the Git repository.
repo_path.title: Repo Path

branch_type.description: Whether to list local branches ('local'), remote branches ('remote') or all branches('all').
branch_type.title: Branch Type

contains.description: The commit sha that branch should contain. Do not pass anything to this param if no commit sha is specified

not_contains.title: Not Contains

title: Git Add
description: Stage files for commit. Add file contents to the staging area (index) to prepare for the next commit.

path.description: Path to the Git repository. Defaults to session working directory set via git_set_working_dir.

paths.description: Array of file or directory paths to stage (relative to repository root). Use ["."] to stage all changes. Paths must not start with "-" — use "./-name" for filenames starting with a dash. Can be omitted when all or update is true.

update.description: Stage only modified and deleted files (skip untracked files).

title: Run read-only SQL
description: Run a SQL statement with no persistent data changes. Always executes inside a `BEGIN READ ONLY` transaction regardless of `ALLOW_WRITES`, so postgres itself rejects any INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DDL and the transaction is always rolled back. Use this whenever the goal is to read - SELECT, EXPLAIN, SHOW, VALUES, WITH ... SELECT, etc. Scope caveat for hosts that auto-allow this tool: `READ ONLY` constrains writes to the DATABASE, not every side effect. Functions whose effect is outside the table data - `pg_cancel_backend` / `pg_terminate_backend`, `pg_read_file`, `lo_export`, `COPY ... TO PROGRAM` - are NOT blocked here and are NOT behind the `ALLOW_WRITES` gate that `pg_kill` sits behind. They still require the privileges the `DATABASE_URL` role holds, so a least-privileged role (e.g. `pg_read_all_data`) is what actually bounds this tool. Use `params` for parameterized queries to avoid SQL injection. Params can be strings, numbers, booleans, null, arrays (for postgres arrays / ANY), or objects (for json/jsonb columns). Large result sets are truncated to POSTGRES_MAX_ROWS (default 1000) with a `truncated: true` flag.

sql.description: The SQL statement to execute. Hard cap of 1 MB.

params.description: Positional parameters referenced as $1, $2, ... in the SQL.

title: Run SQL query
description: Run a SQL query against the configured PostgreSQL database. Postgres itself is the primary safety gate: the role in `DATABASE_URL` enforces what queries can succeed. The recommended posture is a least-privileged role (e.g. one granted `pg_read_all_data`), which makes writes server-rejected regardless of any env var. `ALLOW_WRITES=1` is a secondary belt-and-braces gate - it lifts the in-server `BEGIN READ ONLY` wrapper, but it cannot grant privileges the role lacks. Useful for managed databases where creating a second role is awkward. For read-only access where you want the guarantee in the tool name, prefer `pg_readonly`. Use `params` for parameterized queries to avoid SQL injection. Params can be strings, numbers, booleans, null, arrays (for postgres arrays / ANY), or objects (for json/jsonb columns). Dates and UUIDs can be passed as ISO strings. Large result sets are truncated to POSTGRES_MAX_ROWS (default 1000) with a `truncated: true` flag.

sql.description: The SQL statement to execute. Hard cap of 1 MB.

params.description: Positional parameters referenced as $1, $2, ... in the SQL.

title: Describe table
description: Describe a relation: kind (table / view / materialized_view / partitioned_table / foreign_table), columns (name, type, nullable, default, `generated`, `identity`), primary key, foreign keys (outgoing), `referenced_by` (other tables whose FKs point at this one), `constraints` (CHECK / UNIQUE non-PK / EXCLUDE), indexes, and partition info (`partition_of` parent, `partitions` children). Works on views and materialized views too -- PK/FK/constraint/index lists will simply be empty for a plain view. Use `kind` to disambiguate before assuming you can write to the relation. Generated columns (`generated`: 'stored' / 'virtual') and `identity`: 'always' columns are NOT writable -- omit them from INSERT/UPDATE column lists; a generated column's expression is reported as `generation_expression`, never as `default_value`. On PostgreSQL 18+ constraints also report `validated` / `enforced` / `has_period`, and columns report `not_null_validated` -- a NOT VALID not-null constraint means `nullable: false` can still hide NULLs.

title: Explain query plan
description: Get the query plan for a SQL statement. By default, this uses plain EXPLAIN (no execution). Set `analyze: true` to run the query with EXPLAIN ANALYZE - for non-SELECT statements, ALLOW_WRITES=1 is required (since ANALYZE actually executes the statement). Writes executed during EXPLAIN ANALYZE are rolled back, so you can inspect a plan for an INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE without persisting the rows -- but only what Postgres rolls back is undone: a sequence the statement advanced (nextval, a serial or identity column) stays advanced, and any side effect of a function the statement called that lands outside table data (pg_terminate_backend, an advisory lock) persists. Format is `text` (default) or `json`. Pass the raw SQL (not an EXPLAIN-prefixed statement). Planner options (all optional): `buffers` reports shared/local/temp block hits and is the fastest way to tell a bad plan from a cold cache - it defaults to TRUE whenever `analyze` is true (matching PostgreSQL 18, which turns it on for you), pass `buffers: false` to suppress it; requesting it WITHOUT `analyze` needs PostgreSQL 13+. `verbose` adds output columns and schema-qualified names. `settings` (PostgreSQL 12+) lists planner GUCs set away from their defaults - the usual explanation for a plan that looks impossible. `wal` (PostgreSQL 13+) reports WAL generated and `serialize` (`none`|`text`|`binary`, PostgreSQL 17+) charges the cost of building the result rows; both require `analyze`. `memory` (PostgreSQL 17+) reports memory used by the PLANNER, so it works with or without `analyze` - use it alone to ask why planning a statement is expensive. `generic_plan` (PostgreSQL 16+) plans a parameterized statement WITHOUT values for its $1/$2 placeholders and cannot be combined with `analyze` or `params`. `costs` and `timing` default to true (as in postgres); set either to false to drop those columns, and note `timing` only applies with `analyze`. Options that need a newer server than the one connected are rejected with an explicit error naming the required version instead of a confusing parse failure. Set `hypothetical_indexes` to a list of `{table, columns, using?}` to ask the planner 'what would the plan be if these indexes existed?' -- requires the HypoPG extension (`CREATE EXTENSION hypopg`). The hypothetical indexes are torn down at the end of the call, never touching real disk.

sql.description: The SQL statement to explain. Do NOT prefix with EXPLAIN.

analyze.description: Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE (actually executes the query).

buffers.description: Report buffer hits/reads/dirtied. Defaults to TRUE when `analyze` is true (PostgreSQL 18 does the same); pass false to suppress. Requesting it without `analyze` requires PostgreSQL 13+.

verbose.description: Include output columns, schema-qualified names, and triggers.

settings.description: Report planner GUCs set away from their defaults - explains a weird plan (PostgreSQL 12+).

wal.description: Report WAL generated by the statement. Requires `analyze` (PostgreSQL 13+).

memory.description: Report memory used by the planner (PostgreSQL 17+). Works with or without `analyze`, since planning happens either way.

serialize.description: Charge the cost of serializing result rows (network-bound queries hide it otherwise). Requires `analyze` (PostgreSQL 17+).

generic_plan.description: Plan the statement with UNKNOWN values for its $1/$2 placeholders - the plan a prepared statement would get. Cannot be combined with `analyze` or `params` (PostgreSQL 16+).

costs.description: Include estimated cost/rows/width. Set false for a terser plan.

timing.description: Include per-node actual timing. Setting it to false REQUIRES `analyze: true` (it is rejected otherwise, not silently ignored); false lowers measurement overhead.

params.description: Positional parameters referenced as $1, $2, ... in the SQL.

hypothetical_indexes.description: List of indexes the planner should pretend exist for this EXPLAIN. Requires the HypoPG extension. Indexes are session-scoped and reset at the end of the call.

table.description: Target table. Use `schema.table` (e.g. `public.users`) or just `table` for the search_path.

using.description: Index access method. btree is the right answer for almost every query.

title: Recommend indexes for a workload
description:
Recommend indexes for a workload, and prove each one pays for itself before recommending it. Give it `statements` (the SQL you care about) or let it take the top N from `pg_stat_statements`; it plans each statement, generates candidate indexes, costs them with HypoPG hypothetical indexes, and returns only the ones that measurably cut estimated cost.
How candidates are generated, and the honest limit: this tool has NO SQL parser and does not read your SQL text. It EXPLAINs each statement and harvests the columns the PLANNER reports as filters, join keys, and sort keys, then intersects those tokens with the real column list from `pg_attribute` -- so a candidate can never name a column that does not exist. The extraction is deliberately loose (a token matching a real column name on a different table can slip through); HypoPG is the arbiter, and anything that does not lower cost is discarded. Column ORDER within each candidate is equality columns first (most selective first, from `pg_stats`), then at most one range column, then sort columns.
The search is greedy and BOUNDED. Each accepted index stays in place while the rest are re-costed on top of it, so later picks account for what earlier ones already fixed. `max_candidates` caps how many candidates are considered and `max_explains` caps total EXPLAIN round trips; when a cap stops the search early, `budget_exhausted` is true and the result is a truncated search, not a converged one.
PostgreSQL 18 note, and it reverses a rule you have probably internalized: PG18 added B-tree SKIP SCAN, so a multi-column index whose LEADING column the query never constrains CAN now be used. The classic 'leading column never filtered means the index is useless' heuristic is wrong on PG18+. This tool gates that prune on the server version -- on PG18+ such candidates are kept and costed (`skip_scan_available: true`, and an accepted one carries `requires_skip_scan`), below PG18 they are pruned as unusable and counted in `candidates_pruned_leading_column`.
Requires the HypoPG extension (`CREATE EXTENSION hypopg;`). Hypothetical indexes are session-scoped and are reset before the call returns, on the success and the failure path alike, so they never touch disk and never leak into a later query plan. Statements are only ever EXPLAINed, never executed, inside a `BEGIN READ ONLY` transaction.
Costs are PLANNER ESTIMATES, not measurements: they are the right way to compare two plans for the same statement and the wrong way to predict wall-clock time. They are weighted by `calls` when the workload came from pg_stat_statements, so a query run a million times outranks an identical one run twice. Validate a recommendation with `pg_explain` before creating it, and create it with CONCURRENTLY in production (`create_statement_concurrently`).

statements.description: The workload to optimize. When omitted, the top `limit` statements from pg_stat_statements are used instead (and weighted by their call counts).

limit.description: How many statements to pull from pg_stat_statements. Ignored when `statements` is given.

schema.description: Only recommend indexes on tables in this schema. Candidates elsewhere are dropped.

max_candidates.description: Cap on candidate indexes considered. Candidates are ranked by table sequential-scan count first.

max_explains.description: Cap on EXPLAIN round trips spent searching (baseline plans are not counted). The search stops when the next candidate would exceed it and reports `budget_exhausted: true`.

max_index_columns.description: Widest candidate index to consider. Every narrower prefix is considered too.

max_recommendations.description: Stop after this many accepted indexes, even if more would still help.

min_improvement.description: Fraction of total weighted workload cost an index must remove to be accepted (0.1 = 10%). Relative rather than absolute so it means the same thing on a small and a large database.

title: Database health snapshot
description:
Quick health snapshot: server version, database size, connection counts measured against `max_connections`, active queries with their wait events, a pg_stat_database rollup, and table count. Useful as a connection sanity check and to spot runaway queries, connection-cap pressure, and lock/IO waits.
- connections: `total` for the CURRENT database, broken down into `active` / `idle` / `idle_in_transaction` / `idle_in_transaction_aborted` / `other` (starting, fastpath function call, disabled) / `state_unavailable` -- those six sum to `total`. `idle_in_transaction_aborted` is called out separately because it holds locks and blocks vacuum while doing no work and will never commit. `state_unavailable` counts sessions whose `state` reads NULL because the role lacks pg_read_all_stats / pg_monitor membership; a non-zero value means every other bucket is under-counted by at least that much, so do NOT read `active: 0` next to it as an idle database. Plus `cluster_client_backends` (client backends across ALL databases -- those are what actually consume connection slots), `max_connections`, `superuser_reserved_connections`, and `used_fraction` (cluster_client_backends / max_connections). A raw connection count means nothing without the cap; read `used_fraction` first.
- active_queries: `pid`, `state`, `query`, `application_name`, `backend_type`, `wait_event_type` / `wait_event` (both NULL when the backend is running rather than waiting -- the single most diagnostic pair in pg_stat_activity). Both are reported verbatim as the server spells them, and that spelling changes between majors: a backend waiting on a buffer pin reports `wait_event_type` 'BufferPin' through PostgreSQL 18 and 'Buffer' from 19 on, with the `wait_event` names beneath it changing to match. Read them against the reported `version` rather than hard-coding a literal. `duration_seconds` (since query_start) and `transaction_age_seconds` (since xact_start). A large transaction_age_seconds next to a small duration_seconds is a long-open transaction, the usual root cause behind lock waits, bloat, and stalled autovacuum.
- database_stats: pg_stat_database for the current database -- `deadlocks`, `temp_files` / `temp_bytes` (work_mem spills), `conflicts` (recovery conflicts, only ever non-zero on a replica), `blks_hit` / `blks_read` / `cache_hit_ratio`, and `stats_reset`. Every counter is CUMULATIVE since stats_reset, not a rate -- interpret them against that timestamp.
Sub-queries that fail (several of these are permission-gated on managed providers) append to `_warnings` and leave their field null; the rest of the snapshot still returns.

activeQueryLimit.description: Max active queries to return (default 10, max 100).

title: Top queries by execution time
description:
Top N queries by total or mean execution time. Requires the `pg_stat_statements` extension to be installed and enabled (most managed Postgres providers have it on by default). Returns `{rows, stats_reset, stats_reset_age_seconds, dealloc}`: each row has normalized query text (constants replaced with `?`), call count, total/mean/min/max time in ms, rows returned, and cache hit ratio. Use this to find slow queries worth optimizing.
`calls` and `total_time_ms` are cumulative since the last `pg_stat_statements_reset()`, so this ranking only describes the window that started at the top-level `stats_reset` (with `stats_reset_age_seconds` beside it). This is pg_stat_statements' OWN reset clock, read from `pg_stat_statements_info` -- it is independent of the `stats_reset` reported by `pg_seq_scan_tables` / `pg_unused_indexes`, which comes from pg_stat_database, so do not compare the two timestamps or assume one implies the other. `stats_reset: null` means the start of the window is unknown, not that it covers all time.
READ `dealloc` BEFORE TRUSTING THE RANKING: it counts how many times entries for the LEAST-EXECUTED statements were evicted because more distinct statements were seen than `pg_stat_statements.max` allows. A non-zero `dealloc` means this ranking is drawn from an INCOMPLETE population -- queries may be missing from these results entirely, and an evicted query's counters restart from zero if it runs again, understating it. The larger `dealloc` is, the more churn, so 'not in the top N' stops being evidence that a query is cheap. Raise `pg_stat_statements.max` to get a complete picture.
On pg_stat_statements < 1.9 (before Postgres 14) `pg_stat_statements_info` does not exist, so `stats_reset`, `stats_reset_age_seconds` and `dealloc` are omitted entirely rather than returned as nulls, and a `_warnings` entry says so.
On pg_stat_statements >= 1.10 (Postgres 15+), also returns `io_read_time_ms` and `io_write_time_ms` to separate IO-bound from CPU-bound queries (null when track_io_timing = off or the query did no measurable IO -- enable track_io_timing in postgresql.conf to get non-null values). Scoped to the database in DATABASE_URL: pg_stat_statements is cluster-wide, so results are filtered by `dbid` to match every other tool here rather than leaking query text from unrelated databases sharing the cluster.

orderBy.description: Ranking: total_time (cumulative impact), mean_time (worst per-call), or calls (hottest).

title: Find tables with heavy sequential scans
description:
Tables with high sequential-scan counts relative to index scans - the first place to look for missing-index candidates. Returns `{rows, stats_reset, stats_reset_age_seconds}`: each row has seq_scans, idx_scans, live tuples, and the ratio. A high ratio on a large table usually means a query is reading the whole table where an index would suffice. Pair with `pg_top_queries` to find which query is doing it.
These counters are cumulative since the last statistics reset, so every ratio here is only meaningful relative to the top-level `stats_reset` (and `stats_reset_age_seconds`). A ratio measured over a window that was reset minutes ago describes that window, not the workload; `stats_reset: null` means the start of the window is unknown.
On PostgreSQL 16+ each row also carries `last_seq_scan` and `last_idx_scan` timestamps (null = no such scan since the reset), which separate 'scanned hard months ago' from 'being scanned right now' in a way the raw counts cannot.

schema.description: Limit to one schema. If omitted, all user schemas are included.

minSize.description: Minimum live tuple count to include (default 1000, filters out tiny/empty tables).

annotations.title: Find tables with heavy sequential scans

title: Find unused indexes
description:
Indexes that have never been scanned or have very low usage, largest first. Each unused index costs write amplification (every INSERT/UPDATE maintains it) and disk space, so before adding a new index, check whether the fix is to drop a dead one. Returns `{rows, stats_reset, stats_reset_age_seconds}`.
READ THIS BEFORE RECOMMENDING A DROP: `scans` is a counter, not a verdict. It only counts since the last statistics reset, which is why the top-level `stats_reset` and `stats_reset_age_seconds` are part of the answer. If the counters were reset an hour ago, EVERY index looks unused; if `stats_reset` is null, the start of the window is unknown and the counts prove nothing. This list is only trustworthy once the reset age comfortably exceeds the slowest cycle that could use the index - a monthly report, a quarterly close, a yearly job, a failover-only query path.
PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE indexes are already excluded from these results: they enforce a constraint and stay load-bearing at zero scans, so they never appear here and their absence is not evidence of anything.
On PostgreSQL 16+ each row also carries `last_idx_scan`, the timestamp of the most recent scan (null = never scanned since the reset). 'Not scanned since 2026-02-14' is a far better basis for a decision than a bare count.
On PostgreSQL 18+, do not fall back on the old 'the leading column is never filtered, so this index is dead weight' reasoning. Skip scan lets the planner use a multi-column btree whose leading column is unconstrained, so such an index can now be doing real work.

schema.description: Limit to one schema. If omitted, all user schemas are included.

maxScans.description: Include indexes with scan count <= this (default 10). Use 0 for 'never scanned'.

title: I/O statistics and in-flight async I/O
description:
I/O observability: cumulative per-backend-type I/O from `pg_stat_io` (PostgreSQL 16+), plus in-flight asynchronous I/O handles from `pg_aios` (PostgreSQL 18+). This is the layer underneath `pg_top_queries` and `pg_health` -- it says WHICH subsystem is doing the I/O (client backends vs autovacuum vs checkpointer vs walwriter) and through which path, which a per-query or per-table view cannot.
- io: one row per (`backend_type`, `io_object`, `io_context`) combination. Counters `reads` / `writes` / `extends` / `writebacks` / `hits` / `evictions` / `reuses` / `fsyncs` are bigints returned as decimal strings; `read_time_ms` / `write_time_ms` / `writeback_time_ms` / `extend_time_ms` / `fsync_time_ms` are float8 milliseconds. A timing of 0 next to a non-zero op count means `track_io_timing` is off, NOT that the I/O was free -- turn it on to get real numbers. A NULL counter means the operation is not possible for that combination, which is different from 0.
- io[].read_bytes / write_bytes / extend_bytes: a normalized byte figure that means the same thing on every supported server. On PG16-17 it is computed as `op_bytes * <op count>`; on PG18 `op_bytes` was removed and the server reports bytes directly. The top-level `byte_accounting` field says which source produced the numbers.
- io[].stats_reset: these are CUMULATIVE counters, so a row is only interpretable next to its reset point. Reported per row because that is how the view reports it; `pg_stat_reset_shared('io')` resets them together in practice, but this tool does not assert that.
- Rows whose counters are all zero are omitted by default (`pg_stat_io` is mostly zeros on a quiet system, and the noise buries the handful of rows that matter). Pass `includeZeroRows: true` for the full matrix.
- in_flight + io_method: PostgreSQL 18+ ONLY, and both keys are ABSENT on older servers rather than empty/null -- an empty `in_flight` array would read as 'nothing is stalled' when the truth is 'this server cannot tell you'. `in_flight` is live, currently-outstanding async I/O (`pid`, `io_id`, `op`, `state`, `off`, `length`, `target_desc`), which is what you want while a stall is happening rather than after it. `io_method` (`worker` / `io_uring` / `sync`) explains what `in_flight` can contain: with `io_method = sync` there is no asynchronous submission, so the array is legitimately empty no matter how much I/O is running.
Requires PostgreSQL 16+. Sub-queries that fail (`pg_stat_io` and `pg_aios` are permission-gated on some managed providers) append to `_warnings` and set their field to null; the rest of the response still returns.

includeZeroRows.description: If true, return every (backend_type, io_object, io_context) row including the ones with no recorded activity. Default false -- the view is mostly zeros on a quiet system.

limit.description: Max rows per section (default 200). pg_stat_io has well under 200 combinations, so this effectively bounds the in-flight list on a busy PG18 server.

annotations.title: I/O statistics and in-flight async I/O

title: Inspect blocking locks
description: Show current lock contention: which sessions are blocked and who is blocking them. Returns blocked PID, blocking PID, lock types, relation being contested, and the queries involved. Use this first when a tool call hangs or the app feels stuck - it's the fastest way to identify a long-held transaction holding a lock. Row shape: one row per (blocked_pid, blocking_pid) pair. A session waiting on multiple blockers appears on multiple rows -- group/deduplicate by `blocked_pid` if you want a per-blocked-session count. Scope: CLUSTER-WIDE, unlike `pg_health` active_queries, which is filtered to the database in DATABASE_URL. Lock waits cross databases (a shared catalog, a long transaction in a sibling database), so the blocker is not always somewhere this connection could see -- but it does mean a row here may name a pid in another database entirely. `relation` is only resolved for locks in the CURRENT database or on a cluster-shared catalog (pg_authid, pg_database, ...); it is NULL for a lock held in another database, because a pg_class OID is only meaningful within its own database. A NULL `relation` has TWO unrelated causes, and `lock_type` is what tells them apart. When the wait is ON a relation (`lock_type` relation / extend / page / tuple), NULL means the lock is held in another database and cannot be named from here. When the wait is on something else (`transactionid` / `virtualxid` / `advisory`), `relation` was only ever a best-effort hint -- an alphabetical guess among the blocker's held write-intent locks, not authoritative -- so NULL there means the guess found no candidate, and the blocker is very likely LOCAL. Do not read that second case as 'somewhere else': use `blocking_pid` and `blocking_query`, which are populated either way. Note also that pg_cancel_backend / pg_terminate_backend signal by PID across the whole cluster, so even a genuinely cross-database blocker is actionable via `pg_kill`. Use the blocked/blocking query text to disambiguate which table is actually contested.

title: List roles
description: List database roles (users and groups) with their login/superuser/createdb/createrole attributes and inherited role memberships. Use this to answer 'who has access to this database?' without needing to read `pg_authid` directly.

title: Show table privileges
description: Show which roles have which privileges (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE, REFERENCES, TRIGGER) on a table or on every table in a schema. If `table` is omitted, the result spans every table in `schema`, ordered by table then grantee. Use this to answer 'who can write to this table?' or to audit schema-wide access before a migration. Visibility caveat: backed by `information_schema.table_privileges`, which postgres filters by what the calling role can see. A least-privileged role may not see grants involving unrelated third-party roles. For a complete picture, run as a superuser or a member of `pg_read_all_data`.

title: Cancel or terminate a backend
description: Cancel a running query (SIGINT-equivalent) or terminate a backend connection (SIGTERM-equivalent) by PID. Find the PID via `pg_health` active_queries or `pg_inspect_locks`. Requires ALLOW_WRITES=1 since this changes database session state. The role in DATABASE_URL must have permission - cancelling another user's query needs the `pg_signal_backend` role or superuser. Note: `pg_signal_backend` does NOT cover superuser-owned backends - only a superuser can signal another superuser's session. Cancel is graceful; terminate is forceful. `signaled=true` means postgres SENT the signal, not that the target stopped: a session that is idle (or idle in a transaction) ignores a cancel, so re-check with `pg_health` and use `terminate` for an idle session. `signaled=false` means postgres found no backend with that PID; the `note` field carries its own warning (e.g. 'PID 123 is not a PostgreSQL backend process'). A permission denial is NOT a `false`: postgres raises, so the call returns an error with SQLSTATE 42501 that says what the role lacks.

mode.description: `cancel` aborts the current query; `terminate` closes the connection entirely.

title: Replication status
description: Replication overview: configured replication slots, connected replicas (from `pg_stat_replication`), and current WAL position. Use on primary to spot lagging or disconnected replicas, on replicas to see upstream status. Returns empty arrays on a standalone (non-replicated) database rather than erroring.

title: Database advisor (DBA lints)
description:
Rolled-up DBA lint pass. One call returns four categories of findings:
- sequence_exhaustion: SERIAL / BIGSERIAL / IDENTITY sequences whose `last_value` is above `seqExhaustionThreshold` of `max_value`. The classic incident class.
- wraparound_risk: transaction-ID AND multixact wraparound pressure, the classic pageable incident. `{autovacuum_freeze_max_age, autovacuum_multixact_freeze_max_age, databases[], tables[]}`. Those two cluster GUCs are the divisors both lists are measured against (null if unreadable). Multixact IDs are a SEPARATE 32-bit counter, consumed by row-level locking (`SELECT ... FOR SHARE/UPDATE`, FK checks), so a lock-heavy workload can exhaust them while relfrozenxid stays perfectly healthy -- both counters are checked here. `databases` rows: `{database, xid_age (age(datfrozenxid)), mxid_age (mxid_age(datminmxid)), pct_of_freeze_max_age, pct_of_multixact_freeze_max_age, triggered_by}` -- template databases included, since template0 ages like any other and the cluster horizon is the minimum across all of them. `tables` rows: `{schema, table, relkind, xid_age (age(relfrozenxid)), freeze_max_age, pct_of_freeze_max_age, mxid_age (mxid_age(relminmxid)), multixact_freeze_max_age, pct_of_multixact_freeze_max_age, triggered_by}`, where `freeze_max_age` / `multixact_freeze_max_age` are the EFFECTIVE limits -- a per-table `autovacuum_freeze_max_age` / `autovacuum_multixact_freeze_max_age` storage parameter wins over the GUC. A row is returned when EITHER ratio is at or above `wraparoundThreshold`, and `triggered_by` ('xid' | 'multixact' | 'both') says which one did it: 'xid' means chase freezing/autovacuum, 'multixact' means chase the lock-heavy workload burning members. `mxid_age` and `pct_of_multixact_freeze_max_age` are null on rows whose minmxid is InvalidMultiXactId (no multixact ever recorded); such rows can only be xid-triggered. At pct_of_freeze_max_age 1.0 autovacuum forces an anti-wraparound VACUUM, and near 2.1 billion xids (or 4.2 billion multixacts) the server stops accepting writes. `tables` deliberately includes pg_catalog and pg_toast relations -- the culprit is more often a TOAST table or a system catalog than a user table. On PG18+ table rows also carry `pages` / `all_frozen_pages` / `frozen_page_fraction` from `pg_class.relallfrozen` (visibility-map freeze coverage); those three keys are ABSENT on older servers rather than null.
- tables_without_primary_key: user tables (plain and partitioned) with no PK defined. Bloat candidates and a sign of design drift; some replication setups also need PKs. Foreign tables are excluded -- PostgreSQL forbids declaring PKs on foreign tables.
- public_tables_without_rls: tables in `public` (or any schema in `rlsSchemas`) with row-level security disabled. Useful as a security baseline check.
Any category whose query fails (permission-gated catalogs on managed providers) appends to `_warnings` and returns empty; the other categories still return.
Use this as the 'what should I be looking at?' starting point, then drill into `pg_unused_indexes`, `pg_table_bloat`, `pg_seq_scan_tables` for the perf side.

seqExhaustionThreshold.description: Minimum used-fraction (last_value / max_value) to flag a sequence (default 0.5 = 50%).

wraparoundThreshold.description: Minimum used-fraction to flag a database or table for wraparound risk (default 0.5 = 50%). Applied to BOTH ratios -- age(frozenxid) / autovacuum_freeze_max_age and mxid_age(minmxid) / autovacuum_multixact_freeze_max_age -- and a row is flagged if either one clears it. 1.0 is where autovacuum starts forcing anti-wraparound VACUUMs.

rlsSchemas.description: Schemas where RLS-missing should be flagged. Defaults to ['public'].

title: Estimate table bloat
description:
Estimate table bloat (dead tuples + free space) for tables in a schema. Returns live tuples, dead tuples, dead-tuple ratio, last_vacuum / last_autovacuum timestamps, and total relation size. A high dead_ratio with a stale last_autovacuum is a sign a table needs VACUUM.
On PostgreSQL 19+ every row also carries `stats_reset`: the last time THAT relation's counters were reset via `pg_stat_reset_single_table_counters()`. Read it before trusting anything else in the row -- a reset zeroes live_tuples and dead_tuples AND clears last_vacuum / last_autovacuum / last_analyze together, so a table reset a minute ago is indistinguishable from a pristine one without it. The key is ABSENT on older servers rather than null; null on PG19+ means this relation's counters have never been reset.

Three methods are available via the `method` parameter:
- `estimate` (default): reads pg_stat_user_tables -- fast, no extensions, ANALYZE-driven approximations. Use this first.
- `approx`: uses pgstattuple_approx() -- fast sampling pass, more accurate than estimates, requires the pgstattuple extension.
- `exact`: uses pgstattuple() -- full table scan, exact counts, slow on large tables, requires the pgstattuple extension. Always pass `schema` with method='exact' -- scanning all user tables in one statement will hit statement_timeout on non-trivial databases.
Install pgstattuple with `CREATE EXTENSION pgstattuple` (requires superuser).

schema.description: Limit to one schema. If omitted, all user schemas are included.

minDeadRatio.description: Minimum dead-tuple fraction to include - dead / (live + dead). Default 0.1 = 10%.

method.description: Bloat measurement method. 'estimate' (default) uses pg_stat_user_tables (fast, no extensions). 'approx' uses pgstattuple_approx() (fast sampling, more accurate). 'exact' uses pgstattuple() (full scan, exact but slow). Both 'approx' and 'exact' require the pgstattuple extension.

title: Run read-only SQL
description: Run one read-only SQL statement against the connected PostgreSQL database and get rows back as JSON. Send exactly one statement per call (SELECT, WITH, EXPLAIN, or SHOW). It runs inside an engine-enforced read-only transaction, so any write is refused by the database. Use this tool for all data reading, aggregation, and query planning. Returns {rows, rowCount, returnedRows, truncated}, plus hint when truncated is true. Prefer $1, $2 placeholders with the params array over interpolating values. Results are capped at ~32768 bytes; truncated:true means rows were dropped - add LIMIT/WHERE or select fewer columns.

description: List all tables in a schema (default: 'public'). Use this before querying tables you have not seen yet, then call describe_table for column details. Returns {tables: [name, ...]}.

Locations are script URLs or original source files resolved through source maps (not available with --no-source-maps; scripts in workers and out-of-process iframes are not supported). Stream real-time events from the Docker server, bounded by `limit` events or `timeout_seconds`.

Returns when `limit` events are collected or `timeout_seconds` elapses, whichever comes first
(`limit` caps memory; `timeout_seconds` caps how long the call blocks - without it a quiet daemon
would block indefinitely, since the stream only yields on an actual event).

Caveat for `ssh://` daemons: docker-py can't cancel an SSH stream, so the `timeout_seconds`
watchdog can't interrupt a fully idle stream - bound with `until`/`limit` (or a non-SSH endpoint).

"Wait for the next matching event" idiom: pass `limit=1` with `filters` narrowed to what you
care about (e.g. `{"type": "container", "event": "health_status"}`) and a generous
`timeout_seconds`. This blocks until that one event arrives (or the timeout elapses, returning an
empty list) instead of re-polling a snapshot on a timer. To wait for a state rather than an event
(a container exited or healthy, a service converged), use `system_wait`, which checks the state itself
and so also sees one reached before the call.

Args:
    since: Show events created since this timestamp
    until: Show events created until this timestamp
    filters: Filters to apply to the event stream
    limit: Max events to return
    timeout_seconds: Max wall-clock seconds before returning what was collected

Returns:
    list: A list of decoded event dicts (length <= limit)

Wait until a container/compose project exits or is healthy, a service/stack converges, a node/registry tag is ready.

The one wait tool: action tools return once their work is started (bar `container_exec` and a
timed `container_run`), and this waits for the result. For
a status read without waiting use `container_inspect`, `service_ps` or `compose_ps`; to follow changes
as they happen, `system_events`. Never raises on timeout. `met: false` without `timed_out` means the
condition can no longer be met (the target stopped, has nothing to wait for, or is gone): `detail`
says why.

- container: id or name - not-running (exit code in `detail.status_code`), next-exit, removed,
  healthy (no HEALTHCHECK: not met), log-match (finds `pattern` in recent logs)
- service: swarm manager only; id or name - running (all desired tasks, or `replicas`), update-converged
- node: swarm manager only; id or hostname - ready, down, disconnected, unknown
- stack: swarm manager only; stack name - converged (every service's tasks running, updates finished), removed
- compose: project name from `compose_list` - running, healthy (no HEALTHCHECK: running is enough;
  a job others wait on may have exited 0), exited (exit codes in `detail`); `services` narrows it
- registry_tag: "repository:tag" - present (polls the registry over HTTPS every 5 s by default; no
  daemon, no `host`)

Immediate, with no grace period - prefer `compose_stop` for a clean shutdown (stop signal,

Reverse of `compose_pause`: processes continue from where they were frozen (no restart).

List compose projects known to the daemon (across all directories).

Project-level view (one entry per project); `compose_ps` lists the containers of a single
project.
Raises RemoteFailureError if the CLI call fails.

Args:
    all: Include stopped projects

Returns:
    list: One dict per project (parsed from `--format json`)

Create an immutable Swarm config object; requires a swarm manager.

Configs store non-sensitive configuration files (nginx.conf, app.yaml, etc.) and mount
them into service containers at a specified path. Unlike secrets, config data is not
encrypted at rest - use `secret_create` for credentials or keys. `data` is raw bytes;
encode strings first (e.g. `"my config".encode()`). Once created, a config is immutable:
to update it, create a new config with a new name and update the service to reference it,
then remove the old config with `config_remove`.

    name: Unique config name within the swarm
    data: Raw bytes content of the config file
    labels: Labels to set on the config
    templating: Templating driver config (e.g. {"Name": "golang"} for Go template syntax)

Returns:
    dict: The created config's full document ({"ID", "Version", "CreatedAt", "Spec", ...})

Get a swarm config's full inspect payload by id or name.

Requires a swarm manager. Unlike a secret, a config's payload IS readable after creation:
`Spec.Data` in the result holds the base64-encoded contents. Use `config_list` to enumerate
configs; use this to read one config's contents and metadata.

Returns:
    dict: The config's full document (ID, CreatedAt, UpdatedAt, Spec{Name, Labels, Data base64})

List swarm configs; requires a swarm manager.

Unlike secrets, config attrs include the actual config data (`Spec.Data`, base64-encoded)
since configs are not treated as sensitive. Valid filter keys: `id`, `name`, `names`,
`label` (key or key=value). Fetch a single config by id/name with `config_inspect`.

Args:
    filters: Narrow the list; omit to return every config

Returns:
    list: One full config document ({"ID", "Spec", ...}) per config

Remove a swarm config.

Requires a swarm manager, and fails while any service still references the config - update or
remove those services first. The last step of the rotation flow described in `config_create`.

Returns:
    bool: True after removal

Run a container from an image (create and start in one call, like `docker run`).

Returns once the container has started. For a one-shot command set `timeout_seconds` (with `auto_remove`,
like `docker run --rm`) to wait for it to exit and get its exit code and output; one still running then
is reported `timed_out` and left, never auto-removed: remove it with `container_remove(force=True)`. For
a long job, wait with `system_wait` instead. `container_create` prepares one without starting it;
`container_exec` runs a command in an existing one. Created containers get provenance labels.

Args:
    environment: Environment variables, as `{"KEY": "value"}` or a list of "KEY=value" strings
    ports: Port mappings, e.g. {'2222/tcp': 3333}
    volumes: Volumes to mount, as `{"/host/path": {"bind": "/in/container", "mode": "rw"}}`
        or a list of "host:container:mode" strings
    user: Username or UID to run as
    restart_policy: Restart policy, e.g. {'Name': 'on-failure', 'MaximumRetryCount': 3}
    labels: Labels to set on the container
    auto_remove: Delete the container on exit, logs and exit code included; with `timeout_seconds`, after
        they are read. Not with a restart policy
    privileged: Give extended privileges to the container
    mem_limit: Memory limit: bytes as an int, or a units string ("100000b", "1000k", "128m", "1g")
    cpu_count: Usable CPUs, on a Windows daemon only
    timeout_seconds: Seconds to wait for exit before returning with timed_out=true
    extra_kwargs: Additional keyword arguments forwarded to ContainerCollection.run (call
        `docs_lookup(section="containers")` for the full accepted set)

Returns:
    dict: Without `timeout_seconds`, the started container's full inspect payload; an `auto_remove` container
        already gone returns the payload from before the start, with `removed_on_exit: true`. With it,
        {"id", "name", "exit_code", "stdout", "stderr", "timed_out", "truncated", "removed", "error"}: each
        stream cut at 32 MiB (truncated=true); tty=True puts all in stdout; exit_code null if timed_out;

RestartPolicy.description:
Restart policy for container_run, mirroring the `docker` module's expected dict shape.

Attributes:
    Name: the policy name the docker module expects.
    MaximumRetryCount: how many restarts to attempt, where the policy uses one.

description:
Create a container from an image without starting it.

Use this when you need to configure a container (with `extra_kwargs`) before its first
start, or want creation and start as separate observable steps. For the common case of
create-then-start-immediately use `container_run` instead - it does both in one call.
Start the created container with `container_start`. Common `extra_kwargs` keys: `name`
(str), `environment` (list of "KEY=VAL" or dict), `ports` (dict, e.g. `{"80/tcp": 8080}`),
`volumes` (dict, e.g. `{"/host/path": {"bind": "/container/path", "mode": "rw"}}`), `labels`
(dict). For anything else docker-py's `ContainerCollection.create` accepts, call
`docs_lookup(section="containers")` rather than guessing a key name.

Args:
    image: Image to create the container from, e.g. "nginx:alpine"
    command: Override the image's default command; string or list of strings
    extra_kwargs: Additional docker-py ContainerCollection.create keyword arguments

Returns:
    dict: The created container's full inspect payload (not yet running)

Return the full inspect detail for a single container.

Use this when you need complete information about one container - config, state,
network settings, mounts, environment variables, and resource limits. To enumerate many
containers use `container_list`, which returns this same payload per container only with
verbose=True. For just logs or stats use `container_logs` / `container_stats`.

Returns:
    dict: Full container inspect attrs (equivalent to `docker inspect`)

List containers on the daemon (running only by default).

Pass all=True to include stopped containers. For environment and full config pass verbose=True, or
use `container_inspect` for one container. For a compose project `compose_ps` groups containers by
service; for swarm services use `service_ps` (tasks may live on other nodes).

Args:
    all: Show all containers, including stopped ones (default False: running only)
    since: Only show containers created after this id or name
    before: Only show containers created before this id or name
    limit: Maximum number of results
    filters: Filter by attributes (e.g. status, label)
    verbose: Return each container's full inspect payload instead of its list entry (one inspect call each)
    ignore_removed: With verbose=True, skip a container removed before it was inspected instead of failing
    managed_only: Only return containers created by this MCP server (filters on the docker-mcp-server.managed
        label); combines with any `filters` given

    list: One dict per container: the daemon's list entry by default ({"Id", "Names", "Image", "State",
        "Status", "Ports", "Labels", ...}; a `Status` such as "Exited (3) 2 minutes ago" carries the exit code);
